RESULTADO DEL ANÁLISIS PRINCIPAL (ejecutado) — Hipótesis final en lenguaje natural:

HIPÓTESIS: "Increasing education expenditure (as a share of GNI) is associated with a more favorable —less negative, roughly neutral-to-positive— level of per-capita GDP (GNI pc, constant 2015 US$) in Sub-Saharan Africa than in developing (lower-middle-income) countries. In the pooled panel, the association between education expenditure and log GNI per capita is negative in LMC (developing countries; β ≈ −0.12 to −0.45 per percentage point of GNI), whereas the interaction EduExp×SSA is consistently positive across all specifications (δ ≈ +0.15 to +0.61, p = 0.007–0.178), offsetting most or all of the negative LMC association in SSA (net SSA effect ≈ −0.04 to +0.03, i.e., ≈ 0). In the best-controlled static specification (M2, + secondary enrollment), a 1 pp increase in education expenditure is associated with about −12% log GNI pc in LMC but +2.9% (−0.118+0.147) in SSA (δ = +0.147, p = 0.007); with two lags of expenditure (M4-L2), the lagged-expenditure interaction is +0.606 (p = 0.043), leaving an approximately zero net SSA association. Supporting descriptives: SSA invests a systematically larger share of GNI in education (mean 4.3% vs 3.5%; peak 6.1% in 1997) yet converges toward LMC expenditure levels in 2011–2015 (3.41% vs 3.16%), while its GNI pc remains ~13% higher in level but grows more slowly (+1.25%/yr in 2011–2015 vs +3.3%/yr for LMC). Caveats: these are aggregate (2-unit) time-series associations, not causal effects; SSA GNI is only observed 2011–2015 (no imputation); because expenditure is measured as % of GNI, a mechanical denominator effect can induce negative correlation as income grows; and in the dynamic specification (M5) both short-run effects are near zero. Net: raising education expenditure appears not to be associated with lower per-capita income in Sub-Saharan Africa — in contrast to the negative association observed in developing (LMC) countries — consistent with education spending in SSA being comparatively more tightly linked to (or better buffered in) income outcomes, though statistical power is low."

WORKFLOW EJECUTADO:
1. Carga y reestructuración wide→long→pivot: 82 filas (2 grupos × 41 años, 1975–2015); faltantes = celdas vacías; 0 tokens no numéricos.
2. Estadísticos descriptivos por grupo y ventana (medias, rangos, tendencias lineales, CAGR, picos/valles de EduExp) — 1975–2015, 1991–2015 y 2011–2015.
3. Especificación central (pooled no balanceado: LMC 1975–2015, n=41 + SSA 2011–2015 real, n=5; SIN imputación): log(GNI_pc) ~ EduExp + SSA + EduExp×SSA (M1), + EnrollSec (M2), + ExpGrowth y LabForce (M3); errores HAC (Newey-West, maxlags=1); sin errores clusterizados (solo 2 clusters).
4. Robustez: ventana balanceada 2011–2015 (n=10, 5 por grupo): δ = +0.559 (p<0.001), estable.
5. Endogeneidad/autorregresión: rezagos EduExp t-1 (M4-L1) y t-1/t-2 (M4-L2) con interacción rezagada×SSA; modelo dinámico con logGNI(t-1) (M5).
6. Vía auxiliar (solo apoyo, subordinada): EnrollSec ~ EduExp, 1975–2015 (n=41/grupo), HAC maxlags=3.
7. Limitaciones declaradas en el output.

HALLAZGOS CLAVE (evidencia):
• M1 (n=46): EduExp −0.447 (p=0.082); EduXSSA +0.347 (p=0.178). R²=0.31.
• M2 (n=46): EduExp −0.118 (p=0.007); EduXSSA +0.147 (p=0.007); EnrollSec +0.023 (p<0.001). R²=0.94.
• M3 (n=30): EduExp −0.253 (p=0.036); EduXSSA +0.216 (p=0.011). R²=0.97.
• M1b balanceado (n=10): EduExp −0.659 (p<0.001); EduXSSA +0.559 (p<0.001). R²=0.985.
• M4-L2 (n=42): EduExp_l1 −0.647 (p=0.005); lagXSSA +0.606 (p=0.043) → efecto neto SSA ≈ −0.04.
• M5 dinámico (n=44): EduExp +0.017 (p=0.367); EduXSSA −0.042 (p=0.085) → efectos de corto plazo ≈ 0 en ambos grupos.
• Auxiliar: corr(EduExp, EnrollSec) = −0.35 (LMC) y −0.61 (SSA); regresión SSA b=−7.20 (p=0.011) — signo negativo explicado en parte por el efecto denominador (% de GNI); evidencia de apoyo ambigua, subordinada al estimando central.
• Descriptivos: SSA EduExp media 4.30% (pico 6.10% en 1997, valle 3.10% en 2008, tendencia −0.025 pp/año); LMC 3.50% (pico 3.87% en 1999). GNI pc SSA 1.589 (2011–2015); LMC 1.182 (1975–2015), tendencia +25.5 US$/año.

LIMITACIONES: SSA GNI solo 2011–2015 (sin imputación); panel no balanceado (la interacción puede reflejar parcialmente composición temporal); 2 unidades agregadas → asociacional, no causal; LMC≈países en desarrollo es supuesto; GNI pc como proxy de PIB pc; potencia limitada; "adjusted savings: education expenditure" ≠ exactamente gasto público en educación % del gasto total.

payload.hypothesis: Increasing education expenditure (% of GNI) is associated with a more favorable —roughly neutral instead of negative— level of per-capita GDP (GNI pc) in Sub-Saharan Africa than in developing (lower-middle-income) countries: the LMC main association is negative (beta ≈ -0.12 to -0.45 per pp of GNI) while the EduExp x SSA interaction is consistently positive across specifications (delta ≈ +0.15 to +0.61, p = 0.007-0.178), leaving an approximately zero net association in SSA. Associations only; SSA GNI observed solely 2011-2015; no imputation performed.
payload.workflow: 1) wide->long->pivot melt to 82-row panel (2 groups x 41 years, 1975-2015); 2) descriptive statistics by group and window (means, ranges, linear trends, CAGR, peaks/troughs); 3) central pooled (unbalanced) regressions log(GNI_pc) ~ EduExp + SSA + EduExp x SSA with controls (secondary enrollment, exports growth, labor force participation), HAC/Newey-West SEs (no clustered SEs; 2 units), no SSA GNI imputation; 4) balanced 2011-2015 window robustness (n=10); 5) lagged EduExp (t-1, t-2) with lag x SSA interaction for endogeneity, plus dynamic spec with lagged log GNI; 6) auxiliary supportive analysis of secondary enrollment ~ education expenditure over 1975-2015 (n=41 per group); 7) declared limitations (associational only, denominator effect of %-of-GNI measure, low power).
